Bitcoin energy facts

Short, sourced answers to the questions people most often ask about Bitcoin, energy and the environment. Live figures come from BEEST 2, my tracker of Bitcoin’s energy and emissions, which updates daily. Last updated November 22, 2026.

Energy and emissions

How much of Bitcoin mining runs on sustainable energy?

Most of it. As of November 2026, 60.6% of the energy used to mine Bitcoin comes from sustainable sources (renewables and nuclear), up from 35% in September 2019.

Read more: BEEST sustainable energy chart →

Does Bitcoin waste energy?

No. In fact, it uses waste energy. In Texas, Niaz et al found Bitcoin mining could use up to 93% of the 4.87 million MWh of mostly wind power that was curtailed (thrown away) in 2020.

Read more: The role of Bitcoin mining in climate action →

Why have Bitcoin’s emissions stayed flat while the network grew tenfold?

Because mining machines became more efficient and mining moved to cleaner power. Bitcoin’s net emissions were 36.6 Mt CO2e on November 22, 2019 and 39.7 Mt on November 22, 2026, statistically static, while the computing power securing the network grew more than tenfold.

Read more: BEEST growth chart →

Can Bitcoin become carbon negative?

Yes. On current trends, Bitcoin is projected to go carbon negative between 2031 and 2047.

Read more: Bitcoin could be carbon negative by 2031 →

How does Bitcoin mining cut methane emissions?

By burning gas that would otherwise be flared. Flares leave some methane unburned, and over 20 years methane warms the planet more than 80 times as much as CO2. Bitcoin mining on flare gas already cancels out 4.69 Mt CO2e a year, 11% of the network’s emissions.

Read more: BEEST mitigated chart →

How long do Bitcoin mining machines last?

More than five years. That’s at least 2.76 times as long as the average smartphone (21.7 months), and old machines are then resold or recycled.

Read more: Bitcoin e-waste: what really happens to old Bitcoin mining rigs? →

Why doesn’t “energy per transaction” measure Bitcoin’s footprint?

Because Bitcoin’s energy use doesn’t change with the number of transactions. Four peer-reviewed studies rejected the per-transaction method for this reason, and journalists have since stopped using it.

Read more: Why Bitcoin energy “per transaction” is a spurious measure →

Research and media

Is Bitcoin bad for the environment?

No. In fact, the peer-reviewed evidence points increasingly the other way: 32 papers have found strong environmental benefits. These range from accelerating renewable energy and mitigating methane to reducing the need for gas peaker plants. Between 2018 and 2022, some early reports suggested negative environmental impacts. Two things changed that. First, Bitcoin mining moved to increasingly sustainable power sources. Second, in late 2023, Sai and Vranken found fundamental flaws in the early research suggesting Bitcoin had a negative environmental impact.

Read more: The new (data-backed) story about Bitcoin mining →

Why did the media flip to reporting positively on Bitcoin mining?

Because the research changed first. By May 2025, 80% of recent peer-reviewed papers on Bitcoin and energy found environmental benefits, and 89.5% of mainstream media reports on Bitcoin mining highlighted them.

Read more: Fact and fiction in Bitcoin mining reporting →

Do criminals prefer Bitcoin?

No. In fact, the evidence points the other way. The US Treasury’s 2024 National Money Laundering Risk Assessment, for example, found that “the use of virtual assets for money laundering remains far below that of fiat currency.” In 2025, less than 1% of all crypto transaction volume was illicit, and stablecoins made up 84% of that (Chainalysis). The UN estimates that 2-5% of global GDP is laundered each year (UNODC).

Read more: Do cybercriminals prefer fiat or Bitcoin? →

Grids and power prices

Why are grid operators increasingly using Bitcoin mining on their grids?

Because Bitcoin mines can switch off within minutes when demand outruns supply, which keeps the grid stable. In Texas, every Controllable Load Resource on ERCOT’s grid is a Bitcoin mine, and about 4.6 GW of mining was on the system in 2025 (Potomac Economics).

Read more: AI data centers vs Bitcoin mining →

How does Bitcoin mining help build more wind and solar?

By buying power that would otherwise be wasted, which makes new wind and solar farms more profitable to build. Lal and You, published in PNAS (the journal of the US National Academy of Sciences), found that Bitcoin mining enables capacity expansions of up to 25.5% for solar and 73.2% for wind.

Read more: Bitcoin’s twin revolution →

How can Bitcoin mining lower power prices?

By paying for power, which spreads the grid’s costs across more customers. When a Bitcoin mine left the grid in Hadsel, Norway, in 2024, the grid company lost about 20% of its revenue and raised household bills by more than 20% to cover it.

Read more: How Bitcoin mining keeps energy prices low →

Why did people stop claiming Bitcoin mining destabilizes grids?

Because real events showed the opposite. In the July 2022 Texas heatwave, Bitcoin miners switched off within minutes when ERCOT asked them to, and researchers at Duke and Texas A&M then documented the grid-stabilizing role Texans had just seen.

Read more: Common Bitcoin energy misconceptions →

People

Why is Africa at the forefront of Bitcoin adoption, not the West?

Because Bitcoin solves everyday problems in Africa that most people in the West never face. Sending $200 home to Sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, the highest of any region (World Bank, 2025).

Read more: The untold story about who is really using Bitcoin and why →

Can Bitcoin mining help rural electrification in Africa?

Yes. Gridless, a Bitcoin mining company, has delivered renewable energy to four villages in Africa (an estimated 28,000 people) by buying surplus power from rural microgrids. In Kenya, adding Bitcoin mining to a rural hydro microgrid cut the price of power from 35 to 25 cents per kWh (CNBC, 2024), using hydro energy that was previously wasted.

Read more: 21 Bitcoin use cases already working at scale →

Who is Bitcoin helping most?

People who can’t rely on their banks or their currency. For example, an estimated 329,000 refugees have used Bitcoin to carry their savings across borders and rebuild their lives in a new country (DARI).

Read more: Bitcoin’s value, explained by a refugee →

About Daniel

Daniel Batten in

Author · Environmental campaigner · Climatetech Investor

Daniel Batten has invested in climate tech for more than 20 years and now runs his third climate fund, CH4 Capital. From 1998 until the present day, he has taken part in many environmental actions, including campaigning against native forest logging, anti-GE campaigns, opposing deep sea oil drilling, and exposing Central Bank misinformation against Bitcoin’s environmental merits. In 2023 he helped end Greenpeace USA’s campaign against Bitcoin, which had been heavily influenced by now widely refuted research. In 2025 he personally convinced most mainstream journalists to stop inaccurate reporting about Bitcoin. He is one of the most cited analysts on Bitcoin and the environment. His research has been covered by Forbes, the Financial Times and CoinDesk, referenced by Michael Saylor, and supplied the data behind a Bloomberg Intelligence report on Bitcoin and the environment. This is where he publishes his research.
